conclusion: Therefore the categories necessarily apply to all objects of experience.
label: Transcendental-Deduction
premises: Experience requires that intuitions be unified under concepts.
The categories are the a priori concepts that make such unity possible.

conclusion: Nothing can be conceived as good without qualification except a good will.
label: Good-Will-Argument
premises: A good will is good through its willing, not through its effects.
Every other good (talents, fortune, even happiness) can be put to bad use.
Only a good will is good without limitation.

reference.source: Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals (1785)

conclusion: Therefore we must postulate freedom, immortality, and the existence of God.
label: Postulates-Argument
premises: Practical reason commands us to promote the highest good.
The highest good (virtue with proportionate happiness) must therefore be possible.
Its possibility requires freedom, the immortality of the soul, and the existence of God.

conclusion: Therefore judgments of taste are grounded in a common sense warranting their universal validity.
label: Deduction-of-Taste
premises: A judgment of taste claims the universal agreement of everyone.
It can rest neither on determinate concepts nor on private sensation.
It must therefore presuppose a common sense (sensus communis) shared by all.

reference.source: Kant, Critique of the Power of Judgment (1790)

conclusion: Therefore freedom and natural necessity can both hold without contradiction.
label: Third-Antinomy-Resolution
premises: If appearances were things in themselves, freedom and natural causality would contradict.
Under transcendental idealism, appearances are not things in themselves.
Natural causality then governs appearances, while freedom may govern things in themselves.
